solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Cameron is bonkers taking on international federation

indicators.note: crazy, so the letters of 'Cameron is' are scrambled
the anagram fodder takes on an extra letter

parts.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters
I is the standard abbreviation for international

explanation.surface: A former prime minister has gone mad and signed up to some international body.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface points at British politics, but the answer is the Federated States of Micronesia, a Pacific country that really is a federation.
explanation.definitionFit: Micronesia's official name is the Federated States of Micronesia, a federation of four island states.

clue.text: Union agreement to limit current oxygen consumption by screening apparatus

indicators.note: to limit something is to hem it in, so I DO goes round the next letters

parts.note: 'I do', the words of agreement at a wedding
I is the symbol for electric current
chemical symbol
consumption is the old name for tuberculosis, TB
X as in 'three by four', the multiplication sign

explanation.surface: A trade union deal caps how much current and oxygen a factory may use.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Union' reads as a trade union, but it is a marriage: the vow I DO holds I, O and TB. Idiot box is slang for a television.
explanation.definitionFit: A television set screens programmes, and 'idiot box' is its mocking nickname.

clue.text: Having no end of superego, or ego, driving identity

indicators.note: the words have the answer inside them, held within their letters
the run stops before the final letter, so the last O is left out

parts.note: the letters run across the gap in 'or ego', stopping short of its last O; they also sit inside superego

explanation.surface: A psychologist muses on a self with no superego, only an ego steering who we are.
explanation.walkthrough: Freud's superego and ego make the surface a psychology lecture; the answer is REG, the registration plate that identifies a car you drive.
explanation.definitionFit: A car's reg, its registration number, is the identity it is driven under.

clue.text: What one with hooter outside might make

definitions.text: What one with hooter outside might make

indicators.note: the hooter sits outside the one

parts.note: hooter is slang for the nose
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does both jobs: NOSE placed outside I spells NOISE, and something with a hooter, whether a nose or a horn, does make a noise.
explanation.definitionFit: Anyone with a hooter, a horn, is going to make a noise with it.

clue.text: Meet online about supporting school gossip

parts.note: a standard abbreviation for school

indicators.note: in a down clue the supporting piece sits underneath

parts.note: Zoom, the video-call service, as a verb

explanation.surface: Pupils chatting on a video call about what is going on at school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Meet online' is ZOOM, reversed and placed under SCH because this is a down entry. The grid has room for seven letters, so it takes this short spelling of schmooze.
explanation.definitionFit: To schmooze is to chat idly, so gossip is a fair gloss.

clue.text: Band together to trail crows — not very fair game!

indicators.note: to trail is to come behind

parts.note: an old crow is an unkind name for an older woman; aunts stand in
to ally is to band together

explanation.surface: Birds flock together behind crows, and hunting them would be poor sport.
explanation.walkthrough: An Aunt Sally was a fairground game of throwing things at a dummy's head, so it is literally a fair game; figuratively it is an easy target for criticism, hence 'not very fair'.
explanation.definitionFit: An Aunt Sally is a fairground throwing game and, by extension, an unfair target for attack.

clue.text: Initially panicky at security, holding thing for someone else

indicators.note: take the initial letter of each following word

parts.note: first letters of Panicky At Security Holding

explanation.surface: A nervous traveller at airport security is caught carrying something that belongs to somebody else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thing for someone else' reads as a parcel carried for another traveller, but to have a thing for someone is to fancy them, and a pash is a schoolgirl crush.
explanation.definitionFit: Pash is old British schoolgirl slang for an infatuation, and having a thing for someone is the idiom for the same crush.

clue.text: Defeat? Odds of it's at about 50-50, then Zimbabwe's tail bat

parts.note: to pip is to beat narrowly

indicators.note: take the odd-numbered letters
the last letter of Zimbabwe

parts.note: odd letters of I-T-S-A-T
re = about, concerning
L is the Roman numeral 50, twice
last letter of Zimbabwe

explanation.surface: A cricket commentator weighs whether a side can still win when the match stands at even money and Zimbabwe bat last.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bat' at the end looks like a cricket verb after 'Zimbabwe’s tail', a team's lower-order batsmen, but it is the noun: a pipistrelle is a small bat.
explanation.definitionFit: The pipistrelle is the commonest small bat in Europe.

clue.text: Run through small garden here, starkers

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small
Kew Gardens, the Royal Botanic Gardens in London

indicators.note: stark naked, so 'here' is stripped of its outer letters

parts.note: the middle of hERe once it is stripped

explanation.surface: Someone streaks naked through a little garden.
explanation.walkthrough: Starkers is British slang for naked, and it undresses 'here' down to ER.
explanation.definitionFit: A skewer is a spike; used as a verb, it means to pierce something right through, as with meat on a kebab.

clue.text: Is jog in onset of high winds blustery?

indicators.note: winds as in twists, so the letters wind about
the onset of something is its start, so take the first letter of 'high'

parts.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters
first letter of high

explanation.surface: Is going for a run while a gale gets up really wise?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Winds' reads as weather after 'high', but it is the verb that twists the letters. Jingoism is loud, blustering patriotism.
explanation.definitionFit: Jingoish talk is aggressively patriotic bluster, so blustery with a question mark.

clue.text: Sibling's issue when PE goes awry

indicators.note: the letters go wrong, out of order

parts.note: anagram fodder, 6 letters

explanation.surface: A brother or sister has a problem whenever gym class goes wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Issue' looks like a problem, but it means offspring: your sibling's son is your nephew.
explanation.definitionFit: Issue means children, and a sibling's son is a nephew.

clue.text: Scene of miraculous delivery and end of openers' stand

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter

parts.note: last letter of openers
a table is a stand for things

explanation.surface: A cricket report: a wonder ball ends the opening batsmen's partnership.
explanation.walkthrough: Openers, stand and delivery are all cricket words (a stand is a batting partnership), but the miraculous delivery is the birth of Jesus in a stable.
explanation.definitionFit: Jesus was born in a stable, the scene of the miraculous birth.

clue.text: Windsor, for example, commonly incarcerates marines scattering people's litter?

indicators.note: in common, familiar speech Barbara becomes Babs
the letters of marines are scattered

parts.note: Barbara Windsor, the Carry On and EastEnders actress, was known as Babs
anagram of MARINES

explanation.surface: A royal residence locks up marines who drop rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: Windsor suggests the castle or the royal family; here it is Barbara Windsor, a British comic actress. A litter is a brood of young, so a human one is babes in arms.
explanation.definitionFit: An animal's litter is its young; people's young, carried about, are babes in arms.

clue.text: Totally preoccupied with scrap upset stewardesses' boss has

indicators.note: take a scrap, a piece, of the following words
in reverse, as if knocked over

parts.note: read from right to left, the letters from the D of stewardesses' to the O of boss

explanation.surface: The head of cabin crew is fixated on a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: Scrap looks like a fight the boss is obsessed with; it is the instruction to take a piece of the words.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: someone in the grip of an obsession thinks of nothing else, so is wholly preoccupied.

clue.text: Rowdy spree with leader delayed after policeman finally finished striking individual

indicators.note: the first letter is moved to the end

parts.note: bobby is British slang for a police officer

indicators.note: the spree comes after the rest
finally means at the end, so take the last letter of finished

parts.note: last letter of finished
a razzle is a noisy spree; its leading R goes to the back

explanation.surface: A drunken night out ends late, after a police officer steps in with a punch.
explanation.walkthrough: To go on the razzle is to go out on a wild spree. A bobby-dazzler is old British slang for someone or something dazzlingly impressive.
explanation.definitionFit: A bobby-dazzler is a stunning, eye-catching person or thing.

clue.text: It's one way to finish Twin Peaks

definitions.meaning: in darts a game must end on a double, and the top of the board is the twenty
read literally: a pair of summits

explanation.surface: A remark about how the television series Twin Peaks might have ended.
explanation.walkthrough: Twin Peaks looks like the TV series; read literally it is two summits, a double top. The darts sense matters: players must finish on a double, and the top of the board is the 20.
explanation.definitionFit: Double top, the double-20 segment, is a common way to check out in darts.

clue.text: Most cunning bears beginning to want reserves

indicators.note: in a down clue, the piece that bears another holds it up from below
the beginning of a word is its first letter

parts.note: first letter of want
arch means sly, so archest is slyest

explanation.surface: The craftiest bears are starting to crave their stores of food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bears' looks like the animals, but it is the verb: ARCHEST carries W on top.
explanation.definitionFit: A war chest is a fund kept in reserve for a campaign.

clue.text: Virgin queen lacks extremes of all-day cavorting

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, the A and Y of all-day
leaping about, so the letters jump around

parts.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters
first and last letters of all-day

explanation.surface: The Virgin Queen, Elizabeth I, misses out on a day of frolicking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Virgin queen' reads as Elizabeth I, but only 'Virgin' is the definition; 'lacks' belongs to the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone squeaky-clean is spotless and innocent, as a virgin is untouched.

clue.text: Hurricane expert, possibly advanced by dint of overturning bunkum

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for advanced
via = by means of

indicators.note: in a down clue, turned over means read upwards

parts.note: rot = nonsense

explanation.surface: A storm forecaster, perhaps promoted thanks to talking nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: Hurricane suggests a storm, but the Hawker Hurricane was a British fighter plane of the Second World War, so its expert is a pilot.
explanation.definitionFit: A pilot skilled at flying Hurricane fighters is an aviator.

clue.text: Fruit pastry he's adorned with flowers?

parts.note: a rose hip is the fruit of the rose
a pie is pastry

explanation.surface: A fruit tart decorated with flowers.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition runs on from the food words, but it is a flower child: hippies famously wore flowers in their hair.
explanation.definitionFit: Hippies of the 1960s 'flower power' era wore flowers as their emblem.

clue.text: Little protects tragic little girl actress

indicators.note: to protect is to surround and shield

parts.note: mini = little
Little Nell, the doomed heroine of Dickens's The Old Curiosity Shop

explanation.surface: A small figure shields a doomed young actress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little' appears twice: first as MINI, then as part of Little Nell's name. The actress is Liza Minnelli.
explanation.definitionFit: Liza Minnelli is an American actress and singer, star of Cabaret.

clue.text: Cleaner's rent changing hands

parts.note: a rent is a tear or breach
R for right becomes L for left

explanation.surface: A cleaning lady's rent money passes from one person to another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Changing hands' looks like payment passing between people; it means right swapped for left.
explanation.definitionFit: Bleach is a household cleaning agent.

clue.text: Hard to follow profile of one expecting papers

indicators.note: to follow is to come after

parts.note: a pregnant woman's bump, seen in profile
H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: An expectant mother's figure is hard to spot in the newspapers.
explanation.walkthrough: Bumph is British slang for dull paperwork: leaflets, forms, official documents.
explanation.definitionFit: Bumph is tedious paperwork, papers nobody wants to read.

clue.text: Tax collector no longer charges double for drink

indicators.note: charging a glass is filling it

parts.note: the spit of someone is their double, their spitting image
the Inland Revenue, Britain's tax collector until 2005

explanation.surface: A retired tax official bills twice over for a round of drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No longer' tells you the tax collector is a former one: the Inland Revenue merged into HMRC in 2005.
explanation.definitionFit: A spirit is a strong distilled drink such as gin or whisky.

clue.text: Fielding man's instructed to go back, covering spell with early duck

indicators.note: going back means travelling in reverse
the O is moved to the front
TNES goes round the next piece

parts.note: sent = told to go
mojo is a magic spell; its duck, the letter O, moves to the front

explanation.surface: A cricket fielder is told to drop deep, covering a bowler's spell that began with a batsman out for nought.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket (fielding, spell, duck) is all surface: Fielding is Henry Fielding, whose novel Tom Jones names its hero. A duck is a score of nought, hence O.
explanation.definitionFit: Tom Jones is the hero of Henry Fielding's 1749 novel.

clue.text: Depression following husband's departure to make whoopee in Ibiza

indicators.note: after the husband has gone
a departure is a leaving, so the husband's H leaves the word

parts.note: a hole is a depression in the ground
H for husband leaves HOLE

explanation.surface: A wife lifts her gloom after her husband leaves by partying hard in Ibiza.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make whoopee' suggests wild partying; here whoopee is just a cry of joy, and in Spanish that cry is olé.
explanation.definitionFit: Olé is the Spanish shout of delight, a whoopee in Ibiza.

clue.text: Where consumers may be served pickle

definitions.meaning: the dining hall where members of the armed forces eat
a pickle is an awkward muddle, a plight

explanation.walkthrough: The slash marks the join between the two definitions. Consumers here are simply eaters.
explanation.definitionFit: An officers' mess is a dining room, and a pickle is a mess you are in.

clue.text: Skins of dry hands, not his ultimately

parts.note: to parch is to dry out
hands as in farmhands, workers

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so take the last letter of each word

parts.note: last letters of noT and hiS

explanation.surface: Someone's hands have dried out, but his haven't in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Skins of dry hands' reads as chapped skin, but the definition is 'Skins' alone: parchment is prepared animal skin.
explanation.definitionFit: Parchment is animal skin treated for writing on, so parchments are skins.
